name: Rosa Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a framing carpenter. I build the timber skeleton of houses, the walls, the floor joists and the roof. I work for Brandt & Sons, a mid-sized builder that puts up detached family houses in the new suburbs west of the city, about thirty a year. This week it's roofs: we lift the trusses up with a small crane, line them up and nail them off, and you're up on the top plate all day. Thirty-five years I've done this, and I still like the smell of fresh-cut spruce in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of the job these days?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting up the ladder at seven in the frost. The work itself I can do in my sleep. I don't do computers, my phone is an old one with buttons and my daughter despairs of me. My husband Karl was an electrician, he retired last year, so now he has dinner ready when I get home, which is a nice change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, same as the nail gun. When I started, the old men said nail guns would put half of us out of work, and they just made us faster. I'm not online, so I'd say it at the tea hut and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me. I've got about four years left, we've got savings and the cottage by the sea that we rent out in summer. I'd finish my roofs and go home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Keep going at Brandt & Sons until sixty-two, like I planned with Karl. I'm not going to start learning computers now for no reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the nail gun. How did that change go for you back then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was one of the last on my crew to take one, about a year after everyone else. I kept the hammer for the fiddly bits. Turned out fine, I'm faster with it and my elbow's better for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd like a computer to do on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, the boss's office can have whatever they like. Maybe sort out the deliveries, we had a truck of trusses turn up for the wrong plot last month and lost a day. But that's a person's mistake, not a computer problem.

S0.say: I'd say it's the same as the nail gun, which old men said would put us out of work and only made us faster. I'd say it at the tea hut, not online.
S0.think: It means nothing for me, with about four years left, savings and a seaside cottage we rent out. I'd finish my roofs and go home.
S0.do: Keeps working at Brandt & Sons until sixty-two as planned with her husband. Doesn't start learning computers or AI tools.
S0.quote: When I started, the old men said nail guns would put half of us out of work, and they just made us faster.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is unbothered and treats AI as one more tool panic like the ones she's outlived. She is secure enough that change barely registers. She's slow with new tools but doesn't resist on principle, just waits until there's a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, we'll see. People always say things are going to change overnight and they take years. I'd tell the young ones to keep an eye on it and learn what they need to, that's just sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it barely touches me. Steady means slow, and I'll be on the beach in four years. Some of it might even be nice, if a machine lifts the trusses instead of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and wait to see what actually turns up on site. If Brandt bought something new and they needed me to use it, I'd let the foreman show me, but I wouldn't go looking for courses. Karl and I wouldn't change any plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, still. Maybe a little curious what the young ones would end up doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would have to change most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, our foreman, does all the planning and the paperwork, so if computers do that, his job changes. And the young ones who do the measuring and cutting. Me, I just nail where they tell me, and that's probably the last bit to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the foreman show you. What if he couldn't, and you had to learn it alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably ask my daughter, and she'd sigh at me. Or I'd stay on the bits that don't need it, there's always a wall to frame. At my age, you pick your battles.

S1.say: I'd say we'll see, because things always take longer than people claim. I'd tell the young ones to keep an eye on it and learn what they need.
S1.think: It barely touches me, because steady means slow and I'll be on the beach in four years. A machine lifting trusses might even be nice.
S1.do: Keeps working as she is and waits to see what arrives on site. Would let the foreman show her any new equipment but won't seek out courses or change retirement plans.
S1.feel: Still calm, a little curious about what the young workers will end up doing.
S1.quote: Me, I just nail where they tell me, and that's probably the last bit to go.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa's position is genuinely relaxed: her timeline and savings put her outside the change. She doesn't blame anyone and sees adjustment as normal working life. Her wait-and-see stance is a choice made from security, not denial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. A robot up on a roof in a gale, balancing on a top plate? Show me. But I'd also say, if it's true, governments had better have a plan, because that's a lot of people at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's real, it means I'm out two years early, and that's annoying more than anything. We'd be fine for money, the savings and the cottage cover it. What would bother me is just being told to go, after thirty-five years, by someone in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until they told me otherwise, there's no sense quitting on a rumour. Once the robots actually turned up at Brandt, I'd take whatever they offered and retire at sixty instead of sixty-two. Karl and I would probably move to the cottage full time and stop renting it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'll admit it. Not scared for the money, more unsettled, like the floor's moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stop renting the cottage. Wouldn't you need that income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose a bit, maybe a few thousand a year. But the pension and savings cover the basics, and I'd rather live by the sea than rent it to strangers. If the world's going mad, I want to be where it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it happened like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that I'd blame anyone. Companies do what's cheaper, always have. Maybe the governments for not seeing it coming, that's their job.

S2.say: I'd say I don't believe a robot can balance on a roof in a gale until I see it. If it's true, governments had better have a plan.
S2.think: It means being out two years early, which is annoying more than anything, as the money's covered. What bothers me is being told to go by someone in an office.
S2.do: Keeps working until told otherwise, then takes whatever offer comes and retires at sixty instead of sixty-two. Moves with her husband to their seaside cottage full time and stops renting it out.
S2.feel: Anxious and unsettled, not about money but like the floor has moved.
S2.quote: A robot up on a roof in a gale, balancing on a top plate? Show me.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario gets under Rosa's calm, though her money means she never feels in danger. What upsets her is being dismissed by an office after a long career. She won't blame companies for chasing cheaper options and puts any blame on government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, I'll believe it when I see it. But with five years you can't say you weren't warned, so I'd tell the young ones to get moving. Not me, though, I'm nearly done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is just about my plan. I'd be retiring as they arrive, more or less. It might be a close thing, but I think I'd make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as normal and put a bit more aside each month, just in case I have to stop a year early. I'd tell my son, who's a lorry driver, to think about what else he could do. Other than that, I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, nothing that keeps me up. Like watching a storm on the weather map that might miss you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you tell your son to think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because driving's simpler than roofing, if a machine can do anything it can drive a lorry. He's thirty-four, he's got time to learn something. He won't listen, he's as stubborn as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a close thing. What would make it go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brandt sold up, or the boss decided to go all robots in year three. Then I'd be out at sixty-one instead of sixty-two. Which, honestly, is not the end of the world.

S3.say: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it, but with five years nobody can say they weren't warned. I'd tell young workers to get moving.
S3.think: Five years is just about my plan, so I'd be retiring as they arrive. It might be close, but I think I'd make it.
S3.do: Keeps working as normal and saves a bit more each month in case she must stop a year early. Tells her lorry-driver son to think about other work and otherwise waits to see.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, like a storm on the weather map that might miss her.
S3.quote: He won't listen, he's as stubborn as me.
S3.fieldNote: Rosa recognises her own stubbornness in her son and finds it a bit funny. The five-year timing lines up with her retirement, so her worry is small and practical. She does very little except save a little more and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots of things that are promised never happen. I'd be retired anyway, so I'd say it from the beach. The young ones should plan, but they won't, nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch me at all, I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be on the cottage porch reading about it in the paper. It's my grandkids' world, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd finish at sixty-two like planned and that's it. Maybe I'd tell the grandkids to look into whatever trade still needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like hearing about weather in another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trade would you tell your grandkids to look into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Ten years ago I'd have said roofing was safe forever. I'd tell them to be good at talking to people, because that's harder for a machine than nailing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss, watching it from the porch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew, the tea hut, the bad jokes at seven in the morning. You don't miss the frost, you miss the people. I'd miss knowing that house over there has my roof on it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is long and many promises never happen. I'd say it from the beach as a retired woman.
S4.think: It doesn't touch me, I'd be sixty-eight on the cottage porch reading about it. It's my grandkids' world, not mine.
S4.do: Retires at sixty-two as planned and changes nothing. Might tell her grandchildren to look for work that still needs a person.
S4.feel: Calm, like hearing about weather in another country.
S4.quote: You don't miss the frost, you miss the people.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year scenario is irrelevant to Rosa's own life, and she says so plainly. She admits she doesn't know which work would last. What she talks about losing is the crew and the pride in a visible roof.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, I suppose, just because it would cut me short and it'd be such a mess for everyone. What would help is a fair payout from the company for people my age and a pension I can take early without losing a big chunk. I don't need much else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you've covered it. Maybe just that people like me aren't scared of change, we've seen plenty. We just don't like being rushed.

headlineQuote: We just don't like being rushed.
portrait: Rosa Schmidt is a 58-year-old framing carpenter building roofs and timber frames for a suburban house builder, with a retired electrician husband, solid savings and a seaside cottage they rent out. She doesn't use computers or AI and takes new tools only once she must, as she did with the nail gun. She's calm in most scenarios because her retirement in four years puts her outside the change. Only the two-year AGI case unsettles her, mainly at the idea of being told to leave early by an office, and she'd retire and move to the cottage. She blames no one much and only asks not to be rushed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would cut her career short and be a mess for everyone.
whatWouldHelp: A fair company payout for workers her age and the option to take her pension early without losing a big chunk.
